ladder.why: The purest decision tree: one level per digit, one branch per letter, and a path you extend and shrink as you go.
Each element is in or out, so the leaves of a two-way recursion are exactly the 2^n subsets.
Every slot picks any value not yet placed, so you need a used array that you set before recursing and clear after.

ladder.teaches: combinations with a start index, skipping duplicates
ladder.why: Recursing from the current index (never an earlier one) is what turns orderings into combinations, and staying on the same index allows reuse.

ladder.teaches: combinations with a start index, skipping duplicates
ladder.why: Sorting and skipping an equal value at the same depth removes duplicate combinations without a set.

ladder.teaches: search a grid for a word
ladder.why: Mark a cell on the way in and unmark it on the way out, so one path cannot reuse a cell but another path can.
Only extend prefixes that can still become valid (opens <= n, closes <= opens) and the search never visits a dead string.
Rejecting a column the moment it clashes with an earlier queen cuts whole subtrees, which is what makes backtracking feasible.
A small OA wrapper: permute four digits with a used array, skip equal digits at the same depth, and filter valid times.
Permutations with a neighbour rule checked at placement, so bad branches are never grown.
The choice is where the next piece ends; choose a palindromic piece, recurse on the rest, un-choose and try a longer one.
Assign colors vertex by vertex and abandon a color as soon as a neighbour already has it.

ladder.teaches: search a grid for a word
ladder.why: Word Search without a word: DFS over simple grid paths with mark and unmark, keeping the best length.
Include or exclude each word, pruning a branch the moment two words share a letter (a bitmask AND).
Fill cells with legal digits only, undo on failure, and pick the most constrained cell first to keep the tree small.

notes: All six techniques are covered by clean classics. intuit-n-queens and expedia-palindrome-partitions were in no pool and were added with new solutions. The bank's other Sudoku, Word Break II and account-balancing problems are good extra stretch material. No Amazon OA problem in the pool is genuinely backtracking (the Amazon-tagged candidates are mostly sorting or greedy), so the practice rungs come from other companies' OAs.
